procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal dated April 30, 1962, of Jagdishlal under s. 7 read with s. 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Delhi Municipal Corporation applied to the High Court for special leave to appeal under s. 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which was granted on September 3, 1962. When the appeal (Cr. Ar. No. 163-D of 1962) came up for hearing, the respondent raised a preliminary objection that the Municipal Corporation was not a 'complainant' within the meaning of s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court upheld the objection and dismissed the appeal by its order dated April 29, 1965.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Delhi Municipal Corporation appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment dated April 29, 1965. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and remanded the appeal to the High Court to be heard afresh.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint was invalid because it was not instituted by the Commissioner as required by the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.

facts: A complaint under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 was filed by the Municipal Prosecutor, Shri Sham Sundar Mathur.
The Municipal Prosecutor was authorized to file such complaints by a resolution passed by the Delhi Municipal Corporation.
The respondent argued that the complaint was invalid because, under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, only the Commissioner is competent to institute legal proceedings.
law: The Court acknowledged that Section 476(1)(h) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act gives the Commissioner the power to institute legal proceedings.
However, the Court determined that the present case was governed by a more specific law: Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
Section 20 of that Act states that a prosecution may be instituted by a "local authority" or a person authorized by that local authority.
The same Act defines a "local authority" to include a municipal corporation.
application: The Supreme Court identified the Delhi Municipal Corporation as a "local authority" within the meaning of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
As a local authority, the Corporation was empowered by Section 20 to authorize a person to file a complaint on its behalf.
The Corporation had passed a resolution giving this authority to the Municipal Prosecutor.
Therefore, the complaint filed by the Municipal Prosecutor was done under proper legal authority conferred by the Corporation as permitted by the governing statute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the complaint was invalid. It held that the case was not governed by the general provisions of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, but by the specific provisions of Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Under that Act, the Delhi Municipal Corporation, as a 'local authority', was entitled to authorize the Municipal Prosecutor to file the complaint, which it did via a resolution. Thus, the complaint was properly instituted.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Delhi Municipal Corporation was the 'complainant' within the meaning of s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore competent to file an application for special leave to appeal against the acquittal.

facts: A Municipal Prosecutor, Shri Sham Sundar Mathur, filed a complaint against a respondent under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.
The prosecutor was authorized to file this complaint by a resolution of the Delhi Municipal Corporation (DMC).
The respondent was acquitted by the Magistrate.
The DMC, not the prosecutor, filed an application for special leave to appeal the acquittal in the High Court under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The High Court dismissed the appeal, agreeing with the respondent's objection that the DMC was not the 'complainant' and therefore was not competent to file the appeal.
law: Under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, only the 'complainant' can make an application for special leave to appeal an acquittal in a case instituted upon a complaint.
Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act allows a prosecution to be instituted by a 'local authority' (such as a municipal corporation) or a person authorized by it.

The Court cited the legal maxim: *qui per alium facit per seipsum facere videtur*, which means "he who does an act through another is deemed in law to do it himself." This is the general doctrine of principal and agent.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the individual who physically filed the complaint (the prosecutor) was the only possible 'complainant'.
It reasoned that the prosecutor was not acting in his personal capacity but as an authorized agent of the Delhi Municipal Corporation.
Applying the principle of agency (the Latin maxim), the Court held that the act of the prosecutor filing the complaint was, in the eyes of the law, the act of the Corporation itself.
Therefore, the entity that authorized the action (the principal) should be considered the true complainant, not merely the individual who carried it out (the agent).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Delhi Municipal Corporation must be deemed in law to be the 'complainant' in the case. Consequently, the Corporation was competent to file the application for special leave to appeal the acquittal under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complaint was invalid because it was not instituted by the Commissioner as required by the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957.
appellant_arguments: The complaint was properly filed by the Municipal Prosecutor, who was authorized to do so by a resolution of the Municipal Corporation under Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
respondent_arguments: Under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, the Commissioner alone has the power to institute legal proceedings, including complaints.
This power is exclusive to the Commissioner, and since the complaint was not filed by him, it is invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Delhi Municipal Corporation was the 'complainant' within the meaning of s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore competent to file an application for special leave to appeal against the acquittal.
appellant_arguments: The Municipal Prosecutor, Shri Sham Sundar Mathur, did not file the complaint in his personal capacity but as an authorized agent of the Delhi Municipal Corporation.

Based on the legal principle that he who acts through another acts himself (qui per alium facit per seipsum facere videtur), the Delhi Municipal Corporation should be deemed the actual complainant in the eyes of the law.
As the complainant, the Corporation was competent to file the application for special leave to appeal under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: The complainant was Shri Sham Sundar Mathur, the Municipal Prosecutor, as he was the individual who filed the complaint petition.
Under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, only the 'complainant' is competent to apply for special leave to appeal an acquittal.
Since the application for leave was filed by the Municipal Corporation and not by Shri Mathur, it was not maintainable.

cases.case_name: Ballabhdas Agarwalla v. J. C. Chakravarty
cases.principle: To support the view that where an Act provides a specific machinery for instituting legal proceedings, that machinery must be followed, and such a provision is not merely enabling in nature.
Where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a person is authorized by a legal entity to institute a prosecution, the legal entity itself is deemed in law to be the 'complainant', not the authorized agent who physically files the complaint, based on the principle that an act done through another is the act of the principal.
obiter: Where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a Municipal Prosecutor files a complaint under the authority of a resolution by the Municipal Corporation, they are not acting in a personal capacity but as an agent for the Corporation. Consequently, the Municipal Corporation is deemed in law to be the 'complainant' and is therefore competent to file an application for special leave to appeal an acquittal under s. 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
legal_tests_applied: The principle of agency, expressed by the Latin maxim, 'One who does an act through another is deemed in law to do it himself' (qui per alium facit per seipsum facere videtur).
